# Overview – Stage 6 of 6

Every earlier stage solved a transform and wrote it down. **Stage 6 is the only
stage that applies the whole thing to the point cloud**, in a single pass, and
writes the result to disk.

The composed transform

$$p' = T_z\big(R_{\text{align+xyz}}\, p + t_{\text{align+xyz}}\big) + t$$

where

- $R_{\text{align+xyz}},\ t_{\text{align+xyz}}$ – the **composed** raw -> final
  map recorded at the end of Stage 2 (`R_align_xyz_1` / `t_align_xyz_1`): the
  Stage 1A rough vertical alignment followed by the fine 3D rotation `R_xyz`,
  both about `pivot1`,
- $T_z$ – the Z-only rotation solved in Stage 4, about `pivot1` in XY, rebuilt
  here from the stored `z_rotation_deg` using the identical sign convention
  Stage 5 used,
- $t$ – the XYZ translation: `t_trans_xy` from Stage 5 in X and Y,
  `t_trans_z_applied` from Stage 4 in Z.

Why the ROUGH alignment has to be in there

`las_1` sits on disk in the original scan frame. Stage 1A verticalised it **in
memory only** – there is no `writeLAS` anywhere in Stage 1 – and every
measurement made after that point, `pivot1` and `R_xyz` included, lives in the
aligned frame. So `R_xyz` on its own is a rotation solved for a cloud this stage
never reads. Stage 2 already composed the two legs into `R_align_xyz_1`, and
that is what Step 6.2 applies.

One pivot, so no rotation produces a shift

Stage 1A fixes `pivot1` **before** it rotates and does not recompute it
afterwards, so the rough alignment and the fine `R_xyz` turn about the same
point and their composition is a pure rotation about it. Stage 4 then shifted
the frame vertically and moved the pivot to `pivot2`, and Stage 5 rotated about
that – but `pivot2` differs from `pivot1` only in Z, and a rotation about the
vertical axis is unaffected by a vertical offset of its pivot. `pivot2` sits in
the same place relative to the cloud after the Z-shift as `pivot1` did before
it, so the Z-only leg can be built about `pivot1` and reproduce the staged
result exactly.

The consequence, and the reason it is worth stating: **there is one set of shift
figures, `t_exp`, and nothing else in this stage is a shift.** The translation
columns inside `M_export` are pivot-recentring terms – in UTM coordinates they
run to hundreds of metres for a fraction of a degree – and quoting them as a
"net translation" would be reporting the pivot's coordinates back as though they
were a measurement. Steps 6.2 and the summary each assert that re-expressing the
transform about `pivot1` returns `t_exp` unchanged; if either ever fails, some
leg has acquired a pivot of its own.

Diagnostic toggles

Each transform component can be switched off independently
(`apply_xyz_rotation`, `apply_z_rotation`, `apply_xy_translation`,
`apply_z_translation`). Exporting with a single component enabled is the
quickest way to attribute a residual misalignment to a particular stage.

Export completeness

The export is deliberately **not** restricted to paired or kept trees. Every
point of the source cloud is written, including points whose `TreeID` is `0` or
`NA` (ground, understorey, unsegmented returns). The alignment was *derived*
from a subset of stems; it is *applied* to everything.

# Stage 0 - Setup


## 0.1 Load libraries
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Load libraries and set plot theme"

library(lidR)       # LAS I/O and point cloud processing
library(ggplot2)    # Plotting
library(dplyr)      # Data wrangling
library(plotly)     # Interactive 3D overlay figure
library(base64enc)  # Embed rendered plots into HTML galleries
library(htmltools)  # Assemble the HTML gallery output

# ── Driver-supplied parameter overrides ──────────────────────────────────────
# Every params-* chunk in this file ends with .par_apply("<its label>"). Run the
# file by hand and that call does nothing: the values the chunk just assigned
# stand. Run it under the batch driver, which puts a .batch_params list in the
# environment before the first chunk, and any entry keyed to that chunk label is
# assigned here - AFTER the defaults, so the driver's value is the one that
# survives into the functional chunk that follows.
#
# Why this exists. Parameters used to sit in the same chunk as the code that
# consumed them, so the driver's overrides - which land after a chunk finishes -
# arrived too late to matter, and every pair silently used the .qmd's hardcoded
# value. Splitting each chunk in two fixes the ordering; this helper is what the
# driver reaches through.
#
# The defaults stay in this file rather than moving into the driver. They are
# the single definition, the driver names only what a batch changes, and there
# is no second copy of ~670 parameters to drift out of step with this one.
#
# envir = parent.frame() so a call at chunk top level lands in the environment
# the chunk is being evaluated in - globalenv by hand, the pair environment
# under the driver - without needing .stage_env(), which is defined further down.
.par_apply <- function(label, envir = parent.frame()) {
  bp <- mget(".batch_params", envir = envir, ifnotfound = list(NULL),
             inherits = TRUE)[[1]]
  if (is.null(bp) || is.null(bp[[label]])) return(invisible(character(0)))
  vals <- bp[[label]]
  if (!length(vals)) return(invisible(character(0)))
  if (is.null(names(vals)) || any(!nzchar(names(vals))))
    stop(sprintf("[.par_apply] .batch_params[['%s']] must be a fully NAMED list.", label))
  # A name the chunk did not define is almost always a typo or a rename in the
  # .qmd that the driver has not caught up with. Silence there would mean the
  # batch runs on the default while looking like it was overridden, so it stops.
  unknown <- names(vals)[!vapply(names(vals), exists, logical(1),
                                 envir = envir, inherits = FALSE)]
  if (length(unknown))
    stop(sprintf(paste0("[.par_apply] %s: %d override(s) name nothing this chunk assigns:\n  %s\n",
                        "  Fix the name in the driver's .build_params(), or remove it."),
                 label, length(unknown), paste(unknown, collapse = "\n  ")))
  for (nm in names(vals)) assign(nm, vals[[nm]], envir = envir)
  cat(sprintf("  [params] %s <- driver (%s)\n", label, paste(names(vals), collapse = ", ")))
  invisible(names(vals))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers

# ============================================================
# ggplot theme

theme_set(

# ============================================================
# Stage save/load utilities – shared by every stage file.
#
# Contract (identical in all six stage files):
# SAVE → hard ERROR if any *required* object is missing from the
# environment, so a checkpoint can never be written half-empty.
# A *warning* is raised for any missing *optional* object
# (diagnostic products that may legitimately not have been run);
# those are simply omitted from the file.
# LOAD → never errors on content. A *warning* is raised for each
# requested object that is absent from the RDS. Objects present in
# the RDS but not requested are COUNTED in the summary line and
# never listed. Everything found in the file is loaded either way,
# so nothing is silently discarded.
# PATHS → a save never overwrites: if the target path exists, a numeric
# suffix (_001, _002, ...) is appended until the name is free.
# ============================================================

#' Return `path` if free, otherwise path_001 / path_002 / ... (first free one).
.unique_path <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(path)
  base_noext <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(path)
  ext        <- tools::file_ext(path)
  counter    <- 1L
  repeat {
    candidate <- sprintf("%s_%03d.%s", base_noext, counter, ext)
    if (!file.exists(candidate)) {
      cat(sprintf("Target already exists - using unique name: %s\n", candidate))
      return(candidate)
    }
    counter <- counter + 1L
  }
}

#' Which environment do the stage helpers read and write?
#'
#' A .qmd rendered or run by hand evaluates its chunks in the global
#' environment. The batch driver does not: it gives every LAS pair a fresh
#' environment of its own, so that a leftover object from the previous pair
#' cannot be picked up by one of the exists() guards this pipeline is full of.
#' Under the driver, everything the stages assign therefore lives THERE, and
#' not in globalenv.
#'
#' parent.env(environment()) is the environment this chunk was evaluated in:
#' globalenv() by hand, the pair environment under the driver. It is resolved
#' from where .stage_env was DEFINED rather than from where it is called, so it
#' returns the same environment inside a function as it does at chunk top
#' level, and nothing has to be told which mode it is in.
#'
#' This replaced a hardcoded .stage_env() throughout. Under the driver that
#' pointed at an environment the pipeline had never written to, so every object
#' in a save manifest read as missing and the checkpoint refused to write - the
#' Stage 1 failure that reported 30 missing required objects after a 64-minute
#' fit. (`run_counts` was the one it did find, and only because .tally()'s `<<-`
#' walked past the pair environment into globalenv. That is fixed below too.)
.stage_env <- function() parent.env(environment())

#' Is a batch driver running this file?
#'
#' The driver assigns .batch_mode <- TRUE into the pair environment before the
#' first chunk runs. It changes one thing, and only for the checkpoints: in a
#' batch, every stage runs in ONE session, so Stage N+1 already holds in memory
#' everything Stage N computed and never has to read it back off disk. The
#' checkpoints stop being load-bearing and become a record of the run.
#'
#' So under a batch: nothing in a manifest is required (a missing object is
#' reported and left out, and the pair carries on), a failed write is reported
#' rather than thrown, and .stage_load is a no-op. Run the same .qmd by hand and
#' every one of those is an error again, which is what it should be when the
#' checkpoint is the only thing carrying the stage forward.
.in_batch <- function() {
  isTRUE(mget(".batch_mode", envir = .stage_env(),
              ifnotfound = list(FALSE), inherits = FALSE)[[1]])
}

#' Read one of the driver's batch settings out of the pair environment.
#' Absent - i.e. this file is being run by hand - gives `default`.
.batch_opt <- function(name, default = NULL) {
  v <- mget(name, envir = .stage_env(), ifnotfound = list(NULL), inherits = FALSE)[[1]]
  if (is.null(v)) default else v
}

#' Where a checkpoint goes when a batch is running.
#'
#' Every save chunk in this pipeline assigns its .rds path and then USES it a
#' few lines later, in the same chunk. The driver applies its overrides AFTER a
#' chunk has run, so an override of stage1_rds_path arrives after the file has
#' already been written to the path hardcoded here - which means, without this,
#' every sample in a batch writes over the same hardcoded name.
#'
#' So in batch mode the destination is derived instead, from two values the
#' driver puts in the environment before anything runs: .batch_rds_dir and
#' .batch_sample. The label the save chunk already passes supplies the rest, so
#' "Stage 3.2" becomes <dir>/<sample>_Stage3_2.rds with nothing to keep in sync.
#'
#' NULL means: not in a batch, or the driver did not set the directory - use the
#' path the chunk asked for.
.batch_rds_path <- function(label) {
  dir <- .batch_opt(".batch_rds_dir")
  smp <- .batch_opt(".batch_sample")
  if (is.null(dir) || is.null(smp)) return(NULL)
  file.path(dir, sprintf("%s_%s.rds", smp,
                         gsub("\\.", "_", gsub("\\s+", "", label))))
}

#' Save a stage checkpoint. Errors on missing required objects - unless the
#' batch driver is running this file, in which case nothing is required, the
#' destination is the per-sample one derived above, and a failure to write is
#' reported rather than thrown. See .in_batch() above.
`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

.stage_save <- function(path, required, optional = character(0),
                        label = "stage", envir = .stage_env(),
                        strict = !.in_batch()) {

  required <- unique(required)
  optional <- setdiff(unique(optional), required)

  # A batch may switch an individual checkpoint off by label - the driver's
  # keep_stage3_fit_checkpoint does exactly this for "Stage 3.1", whose chunk
  # must still RUN (the final Stage 3 manifest inherits from it) but need not
  # write a second large file per sample.
  if (!strict && label %in% .batch_opt(".batch_skip_saves", character(0))) {
    cat(sprintf("[%s save] Skipped - switched off for this batch.\n", label))
    return(invisible(NA_character_))
  }

  # inherits = FALSE, matching the mget() below, which has always been strict.
  # With inheritance on, an object could be FOUND in a parent environment and
  # then fail to be FETCHED, and under the driver the parent is globalenv -
  # i.e. the previous pair's leftovers.
  .have <- function(x)
    if (!length(x)) logical(0)
    else vapply(x, exists, logical(1), envir = envir, inherits = FALSE)

  missing_req <- required[!.have(required)]
  if (length(missing_req) > 0L) {
    if (strict)
      stop(sprintf(
        "[%s save] Cannot save - %d required object(s) missing from the environment:\n  %s",
        label, length(missing_req), paste(missing_req, collapse = "\n  ")))
    cat(sprintf(
      "[%s save] %d required object(s) missing - treated as optional and omitted (batch mode):\n  %s\n",
      label, length(missing_req), paste(missing_req, collapse = "\n  ")))
  }

  missing_opt <- optional[!.have(optional)]
  if (length(missing_opt) > 0L) {
    msg <- sprintf(
      "[%s save] %d optional object(s) missing - omitted from the checkpoint:\n  %s",
      label, length(missing_opt), paste(missing_opt, collapse = "\n  "))
    if (strict) warning(msg) else cat(msg, "\n", sep = "")
  }

  present  <- c(setdiff(required, missing_req), setdiff(optional, missing_opt))
  n_opt_in <- length(setdiff(optional, missing_opt))
  dat      <- mget(present, envir = envir, inherits = FALSE)

  # ── The checkpoint describes itself ────────────────────────────────────────
  # The manifest travels INSIDE the file. Without it, loading a checkpoint means
  # first reconstructing the exact `required`/`optional` vectors it was written
  # with - and those are built by chunks, so a later checkpoint could only be
  # loaded after running the chunks that define an earlier one's manifest. That
  # made resuming from an arbitrary point in a fresh session impossible: the
  # Stage 3.2 chunk, for instance, stops outright unless .stage3_1_required is
  # already in scope.
  #
  # Stored under a name no manifest can collide with, and stripped again on
  # load, so it never reaches the session as an object.
  dat[[".__manifest__"]] <- list(
    required = setdiff(required, missing_req),
    optional = setdiff(optional, missing_opt),
    label    = label,
    saved_utc = format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE))

  .write <- function() {
    p <- path
    if (!strict) {
      bp <- .batch_rds_path(label)
      if (!is.null(bp)) p <- bp
    }
    dir.create(dirname(p), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    # .unique_path only interactively. A batch path already carries the sample
    # name, so it cannot collide with another sample, and a re-run of the same
    # sample should REPLACE its checkpoint rather than leave _001, _002 behind
    # for the next reader to guess between.
    if (strict) p <- .unique_path(p)
    saveRDS(dat, p)
    cat(sprintf("[%s save] Saved %d object(s) (%d required, %d optional) -> %s\n",
                label, length(dat), length(present) - n_opt_in, n_opt_in, p))
    p
  }

  if (strict) return(invisible(.write()))

  out <- tryCatch(.write(), error = function(e) {
    cat(sprintf("[%s save] Checkpoint NOT written: %s\n", label, conditionMessage(e)))
    cat(sprintf("[%s save] Batch mode - the objects are still in this session, so the run continues.\n",
                label))
    NA_character_
  })
  invisible(out)
}

#' Load a stage checkpoint. Warns (never errors) on content mismatches, and
#' under the batch driver does not read at all - see .in_batch() above.
.stage_load <- function(path, required, optional = character(0),
                        label = "stage", envir = .stage_env(),
                        strict = !.in_batch()) {

  # In a batch the objects this would read are already live in `envir`, put
  # there by the stage that just ran. Reading them back would at best be a
  # no-op. At worst it would be wrong: checkpoint paths are per-sample and
  # .unique_path() means a re-run writes _001 rather than replacing the
  # original, so the path named here can easily be an EARLIER run's file. And
  # if the write failed or was partial, there would be nothing to read and the
  # pair would die at the start of the next stage having done all the work.
  if (!strict) {
    cat(sprintf("[%s load] Skipped - batch mode: this stage's objects are already in the session.\n",
                label))
    return(invisible(character(0)))
  }

  if (!file.exists(path))
    stop(sprintf("[%s load] File not found:\n  %s", label, path))

  dat <- readRDS(path)

  # ── Prefer the manifest the file carries ───────────────────────────────────
  # A checkpoint written by .stage_save records what it holds, so a load needs
  # nothing from the session - no earlier chunk, no earlier checkpoint, no
  # reconstructed name vectors. `required` and `optional` become a CHECK against
  # what the caller expected rather than the definition of what to read, which
  # is what lets any stage be resumed from any checkpoint in a fresh session.
  #
  # Files written before manifests existed simply have none; those fall back to
  # the caller's vectors, exactly as before.
  mf <- dat[[".__manifest__"]]
  dat[[".__manifest__"]] <- NULL
  caller_req <- unique(required)
  caller_opt <- setdiff(unique(optional), caller_req)

  if (!is.null(mf)) {
    required <- unique(mf$required)
    optional <- setdiff(unique(mf$optional), required)
    src <- sprintf("its own manifest (written %s)", mf$saved_utc %||% "?")
  } else {
    required <- caller_req; optional <- caller_opt
    src <- "the caller's manifest - this file predates self-describing checkpoints"
  }
  expected <- c(required, optional)

  cat(sprintf("[%s load] Reading %d object(s) from: %s\n",
              label, length(dat), path))
  cat(sprintf("[%s load] Manifest: %s\n", label, src))

  # Named by the caller but absent from the file: the real incompatibility, and
  # the only one worth a warning when the file describes itself.
  if (!is.null(mf)) {
    unmet <- setdiff(caller_req, names(dat))
    if (length(unmet))
      warning(sprintf(
        "[%s load] %d object(s) this stage expects are not in the checkpoint:\n  %s",
        label, length(unmet), paste(unmet, collapse = "\n  ")))
  }

  missing_req <- required[!required %in% names(dat)]
  if (length(missing_req) > 0L)
    warning(sprintf(
      "[%s load] %d REQUIRED object(s) absent from the RDS - downstream chunks that use them will fail:\n  %s",
      label, length(missing_req), paste(missing_req, collapse = "\n  ")))

  missing_opt <- optional[!optional %in% names(dat)]
  if (length(missing_opt) > 0L)
    warning(sprintf(
      "[%s load] %d optional object(s) absent from the RDS:\n  %s",
      label, length(missing_opt), paste(missing_opt, collapse = "\n  ")))

  # Unrequested objects are COUNTED, never listed. Every checkpoint from Stage 2
  # onward is cumulative, so this set is routinely hundreds of names long and
  # printing it buried the two messages that actually matter - an absent
  # required object, and an absent optional one - under a wall of text. The
  # count still appears in the summary line below, which is the only part of it
  # anyone reads.
  extra <- setdiff(names(dat), expected)

  # ── Publish what was loaded, for the next stage's save manifest ────────────
  # Every stage's SAVE manifest is built as "the previous stage's manifest, plus
  # my own objects", and the previous manifest is a vector defined by that
  # stage's LOAD chunk. Load a LATER checkpoint directly and that chunk never
  # runs, so the save dies on a missing .stageN_required - which is exactly the
  # resume-from-anywhere case these checkpoints now exist to support.
  #
  # Recording the manifest here breaks the dependency: .manifest_from() below
  # falls back to whatever was actually loaded, whichever chunk did it.
  assign(".stage_last_manifest",
         list(required = required, optional = optional,
              names = names(dat), label = label, path = path),
         envir = envir)

  list2env(dat, envir = envir)

  cat(sprintf("[%s load] Loaded %d object(s) | required present: %d/%d | optional present: %d/%d | unrequested: %d\n",
              label, length(dat),
              length(required) - length(missing_req), length(required),
              length(optional) - length(missing_opt), length(optional),
              length(extra)))
  invisible(names(dat))
}

#' The manifest a save chunk inherits from the stage before it.
#'
#' Looks for the named vector first - that is the normal path, when this
#' session's own load chunk built it. Falls back to the manifest carried by
#' whichever checkpoint was last loaded, which is what makes it possible to load
#' any checkpoint and still save the next one.
#'
#' `which` is "required" or "optional". Stops with something actionable rather
#' than returning character(0): a save that silently inherits nothing writes a
#' checkpoint missing every object from every earlier stage, and nothing would
#' notice until a later stage failed to find them.
.manifest_from <- function(name, which = c("required", "optional"),
                           envir = .stage_env()) {
  which <- match.arg(which)
  if (exists(name, envir = envir, inherits = FALSE))
    return(get(name, envir = envir, inherits = FALSE))

  lm <- if (exists(".stage_last_manifest", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE))
          get(".stage_last_manifest", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) else NULL

  if (!is.null(lm)) {
    cat(sprintf("[manifest] %s not in the session - inheriting from the %s checkpoint that was loaded.\n",
                name, lm$label))
    # For "required", everything the loaded file actually held is the honest
    # inheritance: it is what this session has, regardless of how the file that
    # produced it split required from optional.
    return(if (identical(which, "required")) lm$names else character(0))
  }

  # ── Last resort: the session itself ────────────────────────────────────────
  # No named vector and no checkpoint loaded. That is the ordinary case for a
  # session built by RUNNING chunks rather than by loading - Stage 1 through
  # Stage 3 straight down the document, or an interactive session where the
  # objects were produced rather than read. There is nothing wrong with it, and
  # a save must not refuse.
  #
  # So fall back to what Stages 4 and 5 have always done: take the manifest from
  # the environment. Every non-function, non-dotted object in scope is what this
  # stage inherited, by definition - it is the same rule, just applied later.
  #
  # Only "required" gets this. Optional means "save it if it happens to exist",
  # which is meaningless once the list IS everything that exists.
  if (identical(which, "required")) {
    nm <- setdiff(ls(envir = envir), lsf.str(envir = envir))
    nm <- nm[!startsWith(nm, ".")]
    if (length(nm)) {
      cat(sprintf(paste0("[manifest] %s not found and no checkpoint was loaded - taking the manifest\n",
                         "           from the session instead (%d object(s)). This is the normal path\n",
                         "           when the stage was RUN rather than loaded.\n"), name, length(nm)))
      return(nm)
    }
  } else {
    return(character(0))
  }

  stop(sprintf(paste0("[manifest] %s not found, no checkpoint has been loaded, and the session is\n",
                      "  empty - there is nothing to save. Run this stage's chunks, or load a\n",
                      "  checkpoint, before the save chunk."), name))
}

#' Print the Stage 1 pivot point.
.report_pivot1 <- function() {
  if (exists("pivot1")) {
    cat(sprintf("pivot1 (Stage 1 footprint centre): (%.4f, %.4f, %.4f)\n",
                pivot1[1], pivot1[2], pivot1[3]))
  } else {
    cat("pivot1 NOT available.\n")
  }
}

# ============================================================
# Rotation description: one factorisation, used everywhere
#
# A 3x3 rotation is not readable. Every summary and every error term in this
# stage is quoted as four numbers instead:
#
#   XY rotation magnitude - tilt away from vertical, degrees
#   XY rotation direction - azimuth the +Z AXIS tips toward, CCW from +X, [0,360)
#   Z rotation            - yaw about vertical, CCW seen from above, degrees
#   full XYZ rotation     - the total turn about the matrix's own axis
#
# The first three are an EXACT factorisation, not a description:
#     R = tilt(mag, dir) %*% yaw(z)
# so the three numbers rebuild R to machine precision and .decompose_rotation()
# returns that residual as rebuild_err. That distinction matters for an error
# report - a set of angles that merely characterises a residual rotation is not
# something anyone can act on or re-apply.
#
# The tilt builder is byte-identical to Stage 3's .tilt_rotation_matrix and to
# the one in the test-sample generator. All three must agree: if this stage
# described a rotation in a different convention from the one that generated the
# truth values, the errors below would be measuring the gap between two
# conventions rather than the pipeline's accuracy. Edit one, edit all three.
#
# Convention, verified against the matrix rather than asserted:
#     tilt(m, d) %*% c(0, 0, 1) = (sin m cos d, sin m sin d, cos m)
# so m is exactly the tilt and d is exactly the azimuth the +Z axis leans toward.
# (Points on the ground at azimuth d move DOWN, not up - the axis tips that way.)
# ============================================================
.tilt_rotation_matrix <- function(magnitude_deg, direction_deg) {
  m <- magnitude_deg * pi / 180
  d <- direction_deg * pi / 180
  axis <- c(-sin(d), cos(d), 0)          # horizontal axis, perpendicular to direction
  ax <- axis[1]; ay <- axis[2]; az <- axis[3]
  K <- matrix(c(  0, -az,  ay,
                 az,   0, -ax,
                -ay,  ax,   0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  diag(3) + sin(m) * K + (1 - cos(m)) * (K %*% K)
}

.yaw_rotation_matrix <- function(deg) {
  a <- deg * pi / 180
  R <- diag(3)
  R[1:2, 1:2] <- matrix(c(cos(a), -sin(a),
                          sin(a),  cos(a)), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  R
}

.compose_rotation <- function(xy_mag_deg, xy_dir_deg, z_deg) {
  .tilt_rotation_matrix(xy_mag_deg, xy_dir_deg) %*% .yaw_rotation_matrix(z_deg)
}

#' Exact inverse of .compose_rotation. Returns tilt magnitude, tilt direction,
#' yaw and total angle, plus the residual of rebuilding R from the three.
#' At zero tilt the direction is undefined and returned as NA rather than as the
#' 0 that atan2(0, 0) happens to give - "no tilt" and "tilt pointing due east"
#' are different claims and only one of them is true.
.decompose_rotation <- function(R, dir_tol_deg = 1e-9) {
  m <- acos(max(-1, min(1, R[3, 3]))) * 180 / pi
  d <- if (m < dir_tol_deg) NA_real_ else (atan2(R[2, 3], R[1, 3]) * 180 / pi) %% 360
  M <- t(.tilt_rotation_matrix(m, if (is.na(d)) 0 else d)) %*% R
  a <- atan2(M[2, 1], M[1, 1]) * 180 / pi
  list(xy_mag_deg  = m,
       xy_dir_deg  = d,
       z_deg       = a,
       total_deg   = acos(max(-1, min(1, (sum(diag(R)) - 1) / 2))) * 180 / pi,
       rebuild_err = max(abs(.compose_rotation(m, if (is.na(d)) 0 else d, a) - R)))
}

#' Break a translation into the five numbers the summaries and the error report
#' both quote: the three components, the horizontal magnitude, and the full 3-D
#' magnitude.
.shift_specs <- function(t) {
  t <- as.numeric(t)
  list(x = t[1], y = t[2], z = t[3],
       xy = sqrt(sum(t[1:2]^2)), xyz = sqrt(sum(t^2)))
}

#' The translation a full affine map applies AT a chosen reference point - i.e.
#' rewriting "R x + t_col" as "rotate about P, then shift by s".
#'
#' Needed because a shift is only meaningful relative to a pivot once a rotation
#' is involved. The raw translation column of a world-coordinate 4x4 is dominated
#' by the pivot-recentring terms (these are UTM coordinates, so it runs to
#' hundreds of metres for a fraction of a degree) and comparing two of those
#' tells you nothing. Referred to a pivot, the same matrix reports the metres of
#' shift a reader would recognise.
.shift_about <- function(M, P) {
  P <- as.numeric(P)
  as.numeric(M[1:3, 4] - P + M[1:3, 1:3] %*% P)
}
```
